title: Design In-Memory File System
statement:
Build a class `FileSystem` that keeps a small file system in memory. It begins with nothing but the root directory `"/"`. Every path is absolute: it starts with `"/"`, separates names with `"/"`, and never ends with `"/"` unless it is the root itself. Names use lowercase letters only, and one directory never holds a file and a subdirectory with the same name.

- `FileSystem()` creates the file system with only the empty root.
- `ls(path)`: when `path` is a file, return a list holding only that file's name. When it is a directory, return the names of all files and directories directly inside it, sorted lexicographically (an empty list if it has none).
- `mkdir(path)`: create the directory `path`, which does not exist yet, together with any missing directories on the way to it.
- `addContentToFile(filePath, content)`: if no file exists at `filePath`, create one whose contents are `content`; otherwise add `content` to the end of the file's current contents. The directory that holds the file always exists already.
- `readContentFromFile(filePath)`: return everything stored in the file at `filePath`.

All calls are valid: `ls` and `readContentFromFile` only name existing paths (and `readContentFromFile` always a file), and no path continues below a file as if it were a directory.
constraints: path and filePath start with '/' and do not end with '/', except the root path "/"
Directory and file names contain only lowercase English letters
No directory holds a file and a subdirectory with the same name
mkdir is only called on a path that does not exist yet
At most 300 calls in total are made to ls, mkdir, addContentToFile and readContentFromFile
notes:
## Intuition

A file system is a tree: every directory is a node whose children are keyed by name, and a file is a leaf that also carries text. Storing it as a trie keyed by path segments means every operation is just a walk from the root, one name at a time. A brute force could keep a flat map from full path to entry and scan every key to answer `ls`, which costs time proportional to everything stored.

## Approach

1. Each node holds a `children` map, an `isFile` flag and a `content` string. The constructor makes the empty `root`.
2. `walk(path)` splits the path on `"/"`, drops the empty pieces, and follows (or creates) one child per name, returning the last node. The root path gives no pieces, so it returns `root`.
3. `ls`: walk to the node. A file answers with its own name, cut from the path after the last `"/"`; a directory answers with its children's names, sorted.
4. `mkdir`: walk the path; any missing directories are created on the way.
5. `addContentToFile`: walk to the node, mark it as a file and append `content`.
6. `readContentFromFile`: walk to the node and return its `content`.

## Example 1, step by step

`ls("/")` walks no names and the root has no children, so it returns `[]`. `mkdir("/a/b/c")` creates nodes `a`, `b` and `c`. `addContentToFile("/a/b/c/d", "hello")` walks to `c`, creates `d`, marks it a file and stores `"hello"`. `ls("/")` now sees the single child `["a"]`, and `readContentFromFile("/a/b/c/d")` returns `"hello"`. Output: `[null, [], null, null, ["a"], "hello"]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(L) per call for a path of length L, plus O(k log k) for `ls` on a directory with k entries.
- Space: O(total path names + total content stored).

## Pitfalls

- `ls` on a file returns the file's own name in a list, not its contents and not an empty list.
- `"/".split("/")` gives two empty strings; filter them out or the root lookup breaks.
- Appending must keep the old text: use `+=`, not `=`.
- Sort the names before returning; insertion order is not lexicographic.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `root` | node for the directory `"/"` |
| `children` | map from a name to the child node |
| `isFile` | whether the node is a file |
| `content` | the file's text so far |
| `parts` | the non-empty names of a path |
| `node` | the current node during a walk |

narration.23: Find the node the path names.

narration.35: Walk to the file, creating its node if it is new.
